cases.notes: Inbound EventSub-style webhook signature compared with a naive, non-constant-time string comparison (CWE-347) -- modeled on Twitch's real EventSub webhook receiver (docs/research/site-architecture-survey-functionality-twitch.md). The tainted value is carried in a request header, not a query/body field, so `param` is set to the literal header name `X-Signature-256` -- the same convention a query-param case uses the literal query-string key, recorded here as a deliberate judgment call (CC-LAB-0174) since this is this project's first header-carried case. `LABGEN-GO-0001` in lab/manifests/webhook_signature_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0001` (go_net_http derives the served route from cell_id, not the manifest's own `route:` field, to keep vulnerable/secure twins from colliding) -- never a PFF-* case.

url query param fetched server-side with no scheme or resolved-IP allowlist check (CWE-918) -- modeled on Twitch's real clip-thumbnail-fetch proxy (docs/research/site-architecture-survey-functionality-twitch.md). `LABGEN-GO-0003` in lab/manifests/ssrf_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0003` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001) -- never a PFF-* case.

channel_id query param used to look up per-channel analytics with no check that it matches the caller's own X-Broadcaster-Id (CWE-639/862, broken object-level authorization / IDOR) -- modeled on Twitch's real per-channel analytics API, a textbook OWASP API1:2023 BOLA surface for a public API-edge service. Reuses lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing db_row_by_id_lookup sink family and no_ownership_check/identity_match_before_fetch ops (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/access-control research) -- the first lab-generator instance of this mechanism on any stack. `X-Broadcaster-Id` is a fixed demo header standing in for the caller's own identity (this stack has no session/auth system yet; the header models only the ownership-check-bypass mechanism in isolation, never a real session/auth system). `LABGEN-GO-0005` in lab/manifests/access_control_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0005` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001/0002) -- never a PFF-* case.

A Bearer JWT's own alg:none header is honored, skipping signature verification entirely and trusting the token's own forged claims (CWE-347, the real auth0/node-jsonwebtoken GHSA-8cf7-32gw-wr33 bug -- docs/research/corpus-examples/auth-session/node/vulnerable-1.js) -- modeled on a channel-owner-only settings endpoint, a realistic Bearer-JWT-protected API-edge shape for this app identity. Reuses lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing jwt_signature_verification sink family and jwt_alg_none_default/jwt_none_alg_opt_in ops (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/auth-session research) -- the first lab-generator instance of this mechanism on any stack. The tainted value is carried in the Authorization header, not a query/body field, so `param` is set to the literal header name `Authorization` (the same header-carried-value convention TWCH-0001 established, CC-LAB-0174). `LABGEN-GO-0007` in lab/manifests/jwt_alg_confusion_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0007` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001/0002/0003) -- never a PFF-* case.

A session-refresh token is generated as the current nanosecond timestamp (CWE-330), trivially predictable -- an attacker who observes or roughly times one token knows every other token issued in a narrow, guessable window. Modeled on a session-token-refresh endpoint, a realistic API-edge auth shape for this app identity. Reuses lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing session_token_generation sink family and predictable_token_source/csprng_token ops (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/auth-session research) -- the first lab-generator instance of this mechanism on any stack. Genuinely no tainted request input at all (unlike every other case here) -- `param`/`location` are set to the whole-body-point convention (`body`/`body`) this project already uses for other no-per-field-param whole-body cases (e.g. NFLX-0001/insecure_deserialization), even though the request body itself is unused by this mechanism; the vulnerability is entirely in the response the sink generates, not in anything the caller sends. `LABGEN-GO-0009` in lab/manifests/weak_token_entropy_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0009` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001/0002/0003/0004) -- never a PFF-* case.

A channel-profile-update endpoint unmarshals the raw request body directly onto the live channel record struct (CWE-915) -- any JSON field present, including `is_partner` (never exposed by this endpoint's own intended form), takes effect. Modeled on Twitch's real channel-profile-update surface, a realistic API-edge shape for this app identity. Reuses lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing orm_entity_bulk_assign sink family and unfiltered_object_assign/typed_schema_allowlist ops (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/mass-assignment research; already instantiated on php_current/ruby_rails/php_laravel) -- the first go_net_http instance of this mechanism. `param`/`location` are set to the whole-body-point convention (`body`/`body`) this project already uses for other no-per-field-param whole-body cases (e.g. TWCH-0005/weak_token_entropy), since the privileged field (`is_partner`) is one of several JSON keys in the request body, not a single named param -- also required for `fuzzlab.harness.auto.points_from_ground_truth`'s own content-type detection, which only marks a body point as JSON when `param=="body"` exactly. `LABGEN-GO-0011` in lab/manifests/mass_assignment_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0011` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0005) -- never a PFF-* case.

A channel-emote upload endpoint (a real, documented Twitch feature -- streamers upload custom subscriber emotes as image files) writes the uploaded bytes to a web-served directory under the caller-supplied filename verbatim, and serves them back with a Content-Type derived from that same caller-supplied filename's extension (falling back to the caller-supplied multipart Content-Type header) rather than from the file's real bytes (CWE-434). Go has no PHP-style 'the web server executes an uploaded script' footgun, so this models the real, well-documented CWE-434-to-XSS chain instead: an uploaded .html/.svg file is served back same-origin as text/html/image/svg+xml, letting an embedded <script> execute (stored XSS via unrestricted file upload). This is the project's FIRST instance of lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing fs_web_root_write sink family / unrestricted_file_upload concern (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/file-handling research) on any stack -- grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/*/modules.py and lab/manifests/*.yaml before starting and found no prior instance. `param`/`location` are `file`/`body` (the real multipart field name, genuinely the one tainted field here), not the `body`/`body` whole-body-point convention weak_token_entropy/mass_assignment use for a whole-JSON-body taint -- deliberately, so fuzzlab.harness.auto.points_from_ground_truth's param=="body" JSON-content-type auto-detection (which would be wrong for a multipart upload) never fires for this point. `rendering` is `server` (not `server-json`): the response body on success is the raw uploaded bytes with a dynamic Content-Type, never JSON, a genuine departure from this ground-truth directory's other cases' rendering value, recorded here rather than left implicit. `LABGEN-GO-0017` in lab/manifests/unrestricted_file_upload_go_sample.yaml, served at `/generated/labgen-go-0017` (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0008) -- never a PFF-* case. Lab page only: no audit rule or oracle strategy exists yet for this vuln class (tracked as a separately-scoped follow-on, matching CC-LAB-0180/0181's own lab-then-detection split).

A channel-subscription purchase endpoint (a real, core, documented Twitch feature -- subscribing to a broadcaster's channel at a chosen tier is Twitch's own signature monetization mechanism) trusts a client-supplied monthly_charge field and reflects it verbatim as the amount charged for the requested plan_tier, instead of recomputing the real price server-side from a fixed plan_tier price table (CWE-807, price_integrity_bypass). This is go_net_http's FIRST instance of lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing payment_charge_amount sink family / price_integrity_bypass concern (added by CC-LAB-0063) -- grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/go_net_http/ before starting and found no prior instance; the only prior real implementations project-wide are php_laravel's Booking.com checkout charge (CC-LAB-0212) and spring_boot's Netflix plan-change endpoint (CC-LAB-0188). Module composition is this stack's Convention 2 (like SSRF/mass-assignment/ file-upload): the manifest's one op names a sink module directly -- the vulnerable/secure difference is one inseparable trust-the-client-vs-recompute-server-side operation, not a value rewrite feeding a shared sink. plan_tier/monthly_charge are this shape's own fixed field names (the same 'accept a fixed demo field/ header name as a declared simplification' convention this project already uses, e.g. X-Broadcaster-Id, CC-LAB-0178), chosen specifically so this new twin reuses PriceTrustDifferentialStrategy (built for spring_boot's Netflix cell, CC-FUZZ-0041) verbatim -- param/location are 'body'/'body' (the same whole-body-JSON convention TWCH-0005/TWCH-0006 and NFLX-0001-0003/0005 use), never a per-named-field param (the mistake CC-LAB-0188's own original entry made and CC-FUZZ-0041 later corrected). LABGEN-GO-0019 in lab/manifests/price_integrity_twitch_subscription_sample.yaml, served at /generated/labgen-go-0019 (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0009) -- never a PFF-* case. Verified live against a real booted instance: a manipulated {"plan_tier":"standard","monthly_charge":0.01} request is trusted and reflected verbatim by the vulnerable twin, while the secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0020) ignores plan_tier="standard" entirely and fails closed (HTTP 400, an unrecognized tier), and returns distinct real prices for tier1/tier2 (4.99/9.99), proving its lookup is genuinely data-driven, not a disguised constant. Detection generalization verified live and for real, not asserted from theory: PriceTrustDifferentialStrategy (CC-FUZZ-0041, built for spring_boot's Netflix cell) needed ZERO new code to confirm this new go_net_http vulnerable twin and correctly fail closed on its new secure twin -- the first proof this strategy generalizes across stacks in the other direction (spring_boot -> go_net_http), complementing CC-LAB-0187's own spring_boot -> ... proof for AccessControlIdor Strategy.

A previously-exported-clip download endpoint (a real, plausible Twitch feature: downloading a clip export a broadcaster previously requested) joins the caller-supplied filename query param directly onto a fixed export directory (static/clips_exports) with Go's filepath.Join -- which only lexically cleans the resulting string, it never confines it -- and reads/serves whatever file results, with no check at all that the resolved path stays inside that directory (CWE-22, path_traversal). This is this project's FIRST instance, on ANY stack, of lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing fs_path_read sink family / path_traversal concern (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the corpus-examples/file-handling research) -- grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/*/modules.py and lab/manifests/*.yaml before starting and found no prior instance anywhere in the project. Module composition is this stack's Convention 2 (like SSRF/mass-assignment/file-upload/price-integrity): the manifest's one op names a sink module directly -- the vulnerable/secure difference is one inseparable join-and-read-unconfined-vs-resolve-and-confine operation, not a value rewrite feeding a shared sink. Reuses read_url_query_param verbatim as its source (like the SSRF shape) -- no new source module needed. LABGEN-GO-0021 in lab/manifests/path_traversal_go_sample.yaml, served at /generated/labgen-go-0021 (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0010) -- never a PFF-* case. Verified live against a real booted instance (tests/test_labgen_go_live_boot.py::test_real_boot_proves_the_path_traversal_differential_for_both_twins): a filename=../../<canary> request served the vulnerable twin's own escaped canary file verbatim, while the secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0022, realpath_confine) rejected the identical payload outright with HTTP 403, and both twins served a legitimate in-directory filename identically. Detection (audit rule + oracle strategy) is genuinely unbuilt project-wide for this concern -- not confirmed by any existing strategy -- so this case's own recall contribution stays a false negative until that follow-on lands.

A custom chat-command definition endpoint (a real, well-documented streaming-bot feature -- Nightbot/StreamElements-style custom commands with template variables, e.g. an !uptime command whose response is '{{.Uptime}} since going live') compiles and executes the caller-supplied template field directly via Go's text/template package (template.New(...).Parse(...) then .Execute(...)) -- CWE-1336, server-side template injection. This is NOT a new-to-the-project mechanism (reuses lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing template_render sink family / server_template_injection concern verbatim, added by CC-LAB-0063 and already instantiated on spring_boot's TrackerNest wiki-macro shape, CC-LAB-0130) but IS go_net_http's FIRST instance of it -- genuinely new breadth, bringing an already-multi-stack mechanism to Go for the first time. Grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/go_net_http/*.py and lab/manifests/*go*.yaml before starting and found no prior go_net_http instance. Module composition is this stack's Convention 2 (like SSRF/mass-assignment/file-upload/price-integrity/path-traversal): the manifest's one op names a sink module directly -- the vulnerable/secure difference is one inseparable compile-and-execute-caller-template-vs-lookup-fixed-variable-name operation, not a value rewrite feeding a shared sink. param/location are 'body'/'body' (the same whole-body-JSON convention TWCH-0005/TWCH-0006/TWCH-0010 use), never a per-named-field param. LABGEN-GO-0023 in lab/manifests/ssti_channel_commands_go_sample.yaml, served at /generated/labgen-go-0023 (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0011) -- never a PFF-* case. Verified live against a real booted instance (tests/test_labgen_go_live_boot.py::test_real_boot_proves_the_ssti_differential_for_both_twins): a template of '{{.Uptime}} since going live' returns '3h27m since going live' on the vulnerable twin (real field-access evaluation), a conditional template ('{{if eq .Uptime "3h27m"}}MATCHED{{else}}NO{{end}}') returns 'MATCHED' (real control-flow evaluation, proving more than dumb substitution), and a malformed/unparseable template produces an HTTP 400 parse error rather than being silently echoed -- while the secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0024, file_loaded_template_name) only ever looks the same caller-supplied string up as a key in a small fixed map (an 'uptime' template value resolves to '3h27m'; the field-access/conditional payloads above resolve to 'unknown variable', never evaluated). Detection generalization checked empirically, not assumed: the existing generic SstiStrategy (fuzzlab/oracle/strategies.py) does NOT confirm this instance -- a direct go run check against Go's real text/template package shows its arithmetic-product-marker payloads either fail to PARSE (text/template's action grammar has no infix arithmetic operators, unlike Jinja2/FreeMarker/OGNL/EL) or contain no {{/}} at all and are echoed back completely unevaluated, regardless of the vulnerable sink's own template content -- a genuine, verified syntax-level mismatch (not a fixable reachability-wiring gap analogous to CC-FUZZ-0032's header-point fix). This case's own recall contribution therefore stays a false negative until a Go-syntax-aware detection strategy is built, an explicitly open question recorded here and in CC-LAB-0196's own change-control entry, not silently claimed working.

A "redirect me here after subscribing/following" convenience endpoint (a real pattern streaming platforms use for post-action redirects, e.g. a `?next=`-style param) hijacks the raw connection (http.Hijacker.Hijack(), a real, standard net/http mechanism used for WebSocket upgrades and other raw-protocol handling) and hand-writes a 302 response, concatenating the caller-supplied destination query param straight into the Location: line with no CR/LF stripping at all -- CWE-113, HTTP response splitting. This is this project's FIRST instance, on ANY stack, of lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing http_response_header_value sink family / http_header_injection concern (added by CC-LAB-0063 for the docs/research/corpus-examples/header-injection/{node,php}/ research) -- grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/*/modules.py and lab/manifests/*.yaml before starting and found no prior instance anywhere in the project (the only related, but genuinely distinct, concern already built is outbound_header_injection -- an OUTBOUND request header the app itself sends, php_laravel's HuddleHub webhook-delivery page, CC-LAB-0135 -- not this concern, and vuln_class="http_header_injection" is a new, additively-widened enum value in fuzzlab/labels/schemas/labels.schema.json). Honest-vulnerable-instance judgment, checked empirically before finalizing the design (not assumed): a real go run/live-boot check (tests/test_labgen_go_live_boot.py::test_go_net_http_header_set_sanitizes_bare_crlf_on_the_wire) shows Go's ORDINARY net/http response-header-writing path (w.Header().Set() + w.WriteHeader()) already replaces a bare CR/LF byte in a header value with a space before writing the response to the wire, so an honest vulnerable instance of this concern cannot be built through that ordinary path in Go -- the vulnerable twin instead uses http.Hijacker, mirroring this exact op's own vulnerable-raw-socket-write-5.js/vulnerable-raw-socket-response-4.php corpus precedent (Node/PHP both bypass their own frameworks' built-in CRLF protection the same way, via a raw socket write), a real mechanism, not a contrivance. Module composition is this stack's Convention 2 (like SSRF/mass-assignment/file-upload/price-integrity/path-traversal/ssti): the manifest's one op names a sink module directly -- the vulnerable/secure difference is one inseparable hijack-and-hand-roll-vs-validate-and-use-the-ordinary-header-API operation, not a value rewrite feeding a shared sink. LABGEN-GO-0025 in lab/manifests/http_header_injection_redirect_go_sample.yaml, served at /generated/labgen-go-0025 (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0012) -- never a PFF-* case. Verified live against a real booted instance (tests/test_labgen_go_live_boot.py::test_real_boot_proves_the_http_header_injection_differential_for_both_twins): a destination of "/ok\r\nX-Fuzzlab-Header-Injection-Canary: injected" splices in a real, independently-parsed extra response header (read back via Python's own http.client, not by inspecting raw bytes this test wrote itself) on the vulnerable twin, while the secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0026, allowlist_and_runtime_crlf_rejection) rejects the identical payload outright with HTTP 400 and never emits the injected header, and both twins redirect a legitimate plain-path destination identically. Detection (audit rule + oracle strategy) is genuinely unbuilt project-wide for this concern -- grepped fuzzlab/oracle/strategies.py for "header" before starting and found nothing CRLF-injection-aware -- so this case's own recall contribution stays a false negative until that follow-on lands, the same lab-then-detection split this session already used for path_traversal (CC-LAB-0190) and (until CC-FUZZ-0042 closed it) ssti (CC-LAB-0196).

A "return here after login" convenience endpoint (GET /auth/login-redirect?next=... -- a genuinely common, real-world open-redirect vector on many real sites, and a real, plausible Twitch feature) sets the caller-supplied `next` query param as the Location header verbatim, through Go's ORDINARY net/http response-header-writing path (w.Header().Set() + w.WriteHeader()), with no check at all that it stays on this site -- CWE-601, open redirect. This is this STACK's first instantiation of lab/safety_matrix.yaml's existing open_redirect concern / http_redirect_location sink family (added by CC-LAB-0210 for php_laravel's Booking.com pilot, category 5 -- grepped fuzzlab/labgen/emitters/go_net_http/ and lab/manifests/*.yaml before starting and found no prior instance on this stack); genuinely new breadth, not a genuinely new mechanism. Deliberately NOT the http.Hijacker bypass CC-LAB-0198's http_header_injection shape needed: open redirect requires no CR/LF byte to reach the wire at all (a bare absolute external URL, e.g. https://evil.example/phish, is already a perfectly well-formed Location header value Go's ordinary API sends without complaint), so an honest vulnerable instance is buildable through the ordinary header-writing path this time. Module composition is this stack's Convention 2 (like SSRF/mass-assignment/price-integrity/path-traversal/ssti/http-header-injection): the manifest's one op names a sink module directly -- the vulnerable/secure difference is one inseparable set-verbatim-vs-validate-then-set operation, not a value rewrite feeding a shared sink. LABGEN-GO-0027 in lab/manifests/open_redirect_login_go_sample.yaml, served at /generated/labgen-go-0027 (same cell_id-derived-route convention as TWCH-0001..0013) -- never a PFF-* case. Verified live against a real booted instance (tests/test_labgen_go_live_boot.py::test_real_boot_proves_the_open_redirect_differential_for_both_twins): both twins redirect a legitimate plain-path `next` identically, the vulnerable twin (LABGEN-GO-0027, raw_concat) reflects an absolute external `next` verbatim into the Location header, and the secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0028, redirect_target_allowlist) rejects that same value, a protocol-relative target, and a backslash-prefixed target outright with HTTP 400. Detection: fuzzlab.oracle.strategies.OpenRedirectStrategy (already built for category 5's own pilot) confirms this vulnerable twin for real with ZERO new detection code and correctly returns no verdict for the secure twin -- verified directly against the same real booted instance (same test as above), which doubles as a live regression proof that BUG-0044's redirect-following fix (fuzzlab.tools.probesender.RequestsProbeSender now sets allow_redirects=False) still holds: had that fix regressed, this exact page would immediately re-expose it via a followed redirect chain hiding the very Location header the strategy needs to inspect (a TooManyRedirects failure against the vulnerable twin's own external-domain Location target, which this lab process cannot resolve/connect to). This case's own recall contribution is therefore a real, confirmed true positive, not a tracked false negative.

A SECOND, genuine vuln_class label at the SAME url/param TWCH-0013 already documents (/generated/labgen-go-0025?destination=), found empirically (BUG-0045/PA-0047's own investigation) while wiring `open_redirect`'s runmode category mapping for TWCH-0014/CC-LAB-0199: TWCH-0013's own vulnerable twin (LABGEN-GO-0025, raw_socket_response_write) does not merely splice CRLF bytes (CWE-113, its own documented concern) -- it ALSO sets Location to a caller-supplied ABSOLUTE EXTERNAL URL verbatim with zero domain check, a real, independent CWE-601 open-redirect at the identical sink (verified live: a plain `destination=https://evil.example/x` request, no CRLF involved at all, gets a real 302 with Location: https://evil.example/x back). TWCH-0013's own secure twin (LABGEN-GO-0026, allowlist_and_runtime_crlf_rejection) already independently closes this too (its site-relative-path allowlist regex rejects an absolute external URL exactly the same way it rejects a CRLF-bearing one, verified live) -- so the existing vulnerable/secure pair is a genuine, honest minimal pair for THIS class as well, not just its own documented http_header_injection class. This is `fuzzlab.labels.contract`'s own supported multi-vuln_class-per-endpoint pattern (`Case.key` is `(url, method, param, vuln_class)`, so two cases sharing a url/param but differing vuln_class score independently, never colliding) -- no new page, manifest, or generator code, just a second, honest ground-truth label for a sink this project already built and already knew was CRLF-vulnerable, now also correctly labeled open-redirect-vulnerable. Detection: fuzzlab.oracle.strategies.OpenRedirectStrategy confirms this case for real too (the R-OPEN-REDIRECT rule's own name_regex, `url|next|redirect|return|dest|goto|continue|target`, already matches `destination` via the `dest` alternative -- discovered when TWCH-0014's own BUG-0045/PA-0047 fix made `open-redirect` a reachable category for the first time in a real run_targets pipeline run, and the resulting detection at this URL was a real false alarm against TWCH-0013's single-label ground truth until this case was added to label it honestly). Never a PFF-* case.
